terms.comment: Latin asks the question instead of naming the thing: nēmō scit quis sit, no one knows his identity. For what someone is called, see name.

terms.gloss: the character one presents; a person
evidence: Cic. Clu. 125: quī suppositā persōnā falsum testāmentum obsignandum cūrāverit (M-O s.v. identity)
terms.comment: Literally an actor’s mask, then a role or character, and so a person (Lewis & Short). Suppositā persōnā, under a false identity.
Not in Lewis & Short. Morgan–Owens marks it medieval and notes that it means being the same, as in Dante’s inalterābilis locūtiōnis identitās.

phrases.latin: et dīxī mihi, ‘tū quis es?’ et respondī, ‘homō’
phrases.english: and I said to myself, “Who are you?” and answered, “A man.”

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 331.
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-augustinus), checked against the editions named there.
